summary: Explores issues in using edge computing resources for a media use case involving an Extended Reality application. The application runs on devices of different form factors and needs edge resources to mitigate the effects of limited device capability and latency.

plainLanguage.summary: Headsets for virtual worlds can be too small to do all the work. This looks at letting a nearby computer help so the experience feels smooth.

subtitle: Bringing virtual worlds to life using nearby servers instead of distant clouds

tldr.problem: Extended Reality applications on mobile devices require extreme computational power, drain batteries quickly, generate excessive heat, and need ultra-low latency that cloud servers too far away cannot provide.
tldr.mechanism: Edge computing resources deployed close to users can run the most computationally expensive tasks (scene processing, high-resolution image generation) while devices handle only tracking and display, with tight network timing constraints of 7-15 milliseconds.
tldr.outcome: This use case demonstrates that operators can make XR viable by deploying managed edge services with careful attention to heavy-tailed network traffic patterns and motion-to-photon delay requirements.

today: RFC 9699 is an Informational RFC published in December 2024 and has not been obsoleted. It describes a realistic use case that network operators can use to justify investment in edge computing infrastructure for Extended Reality applications.

sections.title: Extended Reality and Its Challenges
sections.content: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term covering Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Mixed Reality (MR). AR overlays virtual information on the real world. VR immerses the user entirely in a virtual environment. MR exists on a spectrum between them. All forms of XR are computationally intensive: they must process video streams in real time, track the user's head and eye position, build a 3D model of the environment, and generate high-quality video frames to display. This processing generates extreme heat in small devices and drains batteries in minutes. The user's XR headset also needs ultra-low latency—ideally 7 to 15 milliseconds—to prevent motion sickness caused by the delay between head movement and visual response (motion-to-photon delay). Remote cloud servers are too far away to meet these tight timing constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Virtual reality goggles need a lot of computing power and very fast responses. If the response is slow, you feel sick. Cloud servers are too far away, so nearby edge servers have to do the work.

sections.title: The Tower of London Use Case
sections.content: This RFC uses a concrete scenario: tourists visiting the Tower of London wear XR headsets that overlay historical 3D scenes onto their real-world view as they walk around. The application must continuously track the user's position and head orientation, process the surrounding environment to identify which historical scenes to overlay, and generate high-resolution 3D video aligned to the user's viewpoint. This processing must happen in real time as the tourist moves. The XR application runs the less demanding parts locally (tracking and rendering) but offloads computationally expensive tasks (scene analysis and 3D model generation) to edge servers near the historical site. When a sudden surge of tourists arrives, the edge server must handle the load surge smoothly without degrading the experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine wearing goggles that show you ghosts of history while you walk around a castle. The goggles track where you are, and a nearby computer generates the ghost videos and sends them to the goggles to display.

sections.title: Technical Requirements and Constraints
sections.content: XR applications on edge require careful management of three computational tasks: tracking (measuring head and eye position in 3D space), world modeling (building a 3D representation of the environment), and registration (aligning virtual objects with real-world features, including color and lighting). The motion-to-photon delay budget is 20 milliseconds maximum. Of this, display hardware consumes 12-13 milliseconds, leaving 7-8 milliseconds for sensor processing, rendering, and network round-trip time. Edge servers must be deployed with minimal network latency—the RFC cites a 3GPP target of 0.1 to 1 millisecond round-trip latency between edge and user. The downlink bandwidth requirement is enormous: a 6 degrees-of-freedom (6DoF) video stream requires 200 to 1000 Mbps, compared to 2 Mbps for video conferencing or 10-50 Mbps for 4K 360-degree video.
sections.plainLanguage: The goggles need to show new pictures every few milliseconds or you will feel sick. The network has to send a huge amount of data very fast—a hundred to a thousand times faster than a video call.

sections.title: Traffic Characteristics and Network Behavior
sections.content: XR traffic exhibits heavy-tailed distributions in parameters such as buffer occupancy, throughput, and latency. Unlike predictable on-demand video, XR traffic shows sudden surges when a group of users joins, exhibits long-range dependencies where events far apart are correlated, and contains self-similar bursts at multiple timescales. Multi-fractal spectrum bursts at millisecond timescales can induce jitter that causes motion sickness. Standard Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) algorithms that rely on mean and standard deviation fail with heavy-tailed distributions because the mean takes too long to stabilize and the expectation paradox—the longer you wait, the longer you expect to wait—makes prediction unreliable. Network operators must deploy managed edge cloud services with dynamic server placement, mobility support, energy management, and quality assurance mechanisms such as differentiated services (DiffServ) or RSVP-based per-connection QoS.
sections.plainLanguage: When a group shows up, a lot of people tune in at once, and traffic becomes unpredictable. Standard formulas for adapting bitrate do not work well with this kind of bursty traffic, so operators need smarter network management.

sections.title: Operational Deployment Strategy
sections.content: To operationalize an XR use case like this, a network operator must provide a high-capacity, low-latency path from edge servers to the mobile devices running XR applications. The operator must provision edge server capacity, CPU and GPU resources, and bandwidth sufficient to handle the maximum expected number of simultaneous users. The operator must understand the bandwidth and response time requirements of the specific application. For the Tower of London example, 200 to 1000 Mbps per user and a 7-15 millisecond response time are the targets. The operator must also consider economic viability: the cost of deploying edge infrastructure must be justified by the revenue from new XR applications. As edge servers are inherently limited in capacity compared to distant cloud, the operator must use careful resource management and billing models to ensure sustainable operations.
sections.plainLanguage: To offer this service, a network operator has to build computers nearby, give them enough power and bandwidth, and charge enough money to pay for it all. They also need to make sure the system does not get overloaded when a lot of people show up at once.

items.title: Motion-to-Photon Delay
items.text: Must stay below 20 ms, ideally 7-15 ms, to avoid motion sickness

items.title: Massive Bandwidth
items.text: 200 to 1000 Mbps per user; 100 to 1000 times higher than video calls

items.title: Heavy-Tailed Traffic
items.text: Sudden bursts when groups arrive; unpredictable; breaks standard adaptation algorithms

items.title: Heat and Battery
items.text: Local computation drains batteries and generates dangerous heat in headsets
